prerequisites: Mathematics I and II from high school
Good command of matrix calculus at high school level

learning_outcomes.text: Choose and apply the most suitable methods and techniques to analyze and solve problems defined by data that represent a challenge due to their volume, velocity, variety or heterogeneity, including computational, mathematical, statistical and signal processing methods.

Have the experimental and analytical skills to work autonomously, being able to design experiments and to describe, analyze, evaluate and interpret the resulting information to propose alternative and novel solutions to known and/or emerging problems.
Create models and make decisions based on available data combining acquired knowledge and being able to apply new ones to problem solving.
Ability to integrate into a multidisciplinary team within the framework of a data science project.
Ability to express data processing results clearly and convincingly both in writing and orally.

Students have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in a field of study that builds on general secondary education, and is usually found at a level that, while supported by advanced textbooks, also includes some aspects that imply knowledge from the forefront of their field of study.

Students know how to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional way and possess the competencies that are usually demonstrated by elaborating and defending arguments and solving problems within their area of study.
Students have the ability to gather and interpret relevant data (usually within their field of study) to make judgments that include reflection on relevant social, scientific or ethical issues.
Students can transmit information, ideas, problems and solutions to both specialized and non-specialized audiences.
Students have developed the learning skills necessary to undertake further studies with a high degree of autonomy.

Know the appropriate mathematical concepts and methods to obtain models capable of solving problems that may arise in the context of data science and engineering: linear algebra, differential and integral calculus.
Use the basic elements of Linear Algebra: systems of linear equations, vector spaces and linear applications, and use matrices to simplify their study.
Analyze and apply numerical methods for solving systems of linear equations.
Be able to calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors and diagonalize endomorphisms and matrices.
Apply diagonalization methods for solving discrete linear dynamic systems.
Use numerical methods to calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
Use computer tools for solving Linear Algebra problems.

syllabus_topics: Matrices
Definition and operations with matrices
Types of matrices
Elementary transformations of matrices: matrix associated with a given one
LU factorization of a matrix
Linear systems, numerical methods of resolution
Matrix form of a system of equations
Gaussian elimination: discussion and resolution of systems of linear equations
Relative and absolute errors: matrix norms
Numerical methods for solving systems: Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel methods
Vector spaces
Notion of vector space
Vectors, linear combinations, dependence, generators, bases, coordinates
Vector subspaces, intersection and sum
Linear applications
Definition and properties of linear applications
Matrix associated with a linear application, kernel and image, rank
Change of basis. Similar matrices
Diagonalization
Definition of eigenvalues and eigenvectors associated with a matrix
Diagonalization of matrices: necessary and sufficient conditions for diagonalization
Equivalent matrices
Discrete linear dynamic systems
Recurrence relations
Different types of discrete linear dynamic systems
Matrix resolution
Numerical methods for calculating eigenvectors and eigenvalues
Power method
Inverse power method
Introduction to MATLAB: Numeric and symbolic variables, symbolic functions, vectors and matrices
Matrices and systems: operations. The rref, linspace, a:h:b etc commands
Numerical methods for solving systems: Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel algorithms: Creation of function files. Calculation of vector and matrix norms. Relative, absolute and percentage errors
Vector spaces and linear applications
Endomorphisms: diagonalization. eig, poly, roots, etc. instructions
Discrete dynamic systems
Numerical methods for calculating eigenvalues and eigenvectors: Power and inverse power methods
teaching_methods: Online teaching (videos, presentations, instructional texts, self-assessment questionnaires)
Consultations via Teams chat, Virtual Campus forums, or individual/group virtual tutorials
assessment_rules: The final grade (NF) for the course is calculated as NF = 0.5*NE + 0.2*NL + 0.2*PA + 0.1*NCv, where NE is the average of written controls (P1 and P2), NL is the lab practice grade, PA is the classroom work and tutoring grade, and NCv is the virtual campus activities grade. To pass, NF must be >= 5, and NL and NE must both be >= 3.5. If these minimums are not met, the final grade will be the minimum of NF and 4.5. Students who do not attend the ordinary exam will be marked as "No presentado". For extraordinary calls, students can retake written (NE) and lab practice (NL) exams; the final grade formula NF = 0.7*NE + 0.2*NL + 0.1*NCv (or NOL for differentiated evaluation) is used, with NL and NCv/NOL carried over from the ordinary call if not retaken. If cheating is detected, the grade for the corresponding assessment will be 0 points, and the School of Engineering will be informed.
